positions.commentary: The speaker states that if NVIDIA ends up being a $10 trillion company in 10 years, he doesn't really lose anything for not investing, but also acknowledges it could be less.
The speaker questions the relevance of ESG, stating that Tesla is considered a bad company while some oil refiners are considered good.
The speaker suggests keeping an existing investment in Microsoft but notes difficulty paying up for it at current prices, and avoids making new investment recommendations on AI race winners.
The speaker lists Cisco as one of the top three most valuable companies in the world in early 2000, along with Microsoft and General Electric, but notes none would have been a great investment.

thesis: This episode argues that current market valuations for tech giants like NVIDIA and Microsoft are difficult to justify using traditional discounted cash flow models and are driven by market euphoria rather than fundamental certainty. The speaker uses historical parallels to the dot-com bubble of 2000 to illustrate that while these companies are excellent businesses, investing at these levels carries high error rates and potential for significant drawdowns, as seen with Microsoft's performance from 2000 to 2013. The thesis is thin, focusing primarily on valuation skepticism and the dangers of market timing rather than a specific investment strategy.

claims.quote: And when I look at the NVIDIA situation today, to me, it rhymes a lot with the way Microsoft was at that time. It was just, you know, so the blue chips, the blue chips, great business, recovering revenues.

claims.claim: The speaker states that if NVIDIA ends up being a $10 trillion company in 10 years, he doesn't really lose anything for not investing, but also acknowledges it could be less.
claims.quote: So if I don't make an investment in NVIDIA, and NVIDIA ends up being a $10 trillion company, 10 years from now, I don't really lose anything. Yes, I didn't make that 10x. But what matters is what I actually invested in, what happened with those things.

claims.claim: The speaker recalls that Microsoft's market cap was over 600 billion in early 2000, making it one of the top three most valuable companies in the world, but it was not a great investment.
claims.quote: And when I looked at the Microsoft market cap at that time in early 2000, it was over 600 billion. It was in the top three most valuable companies in the world at that time. The top three most valuable companies was Cisco, Microsoft, and General Electric. None of those would have been a great investment.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Microsoft never saw that 600 billion market cap for the next 13 years and took a huge drawdown to less than 100 billion.
claims.quote: Microsoft never saw that 600 billion market cap for the next 13 years. And in fact, it took a huge drawdown. I mean, the 600 billion went down to, I think, less than 100 billion or so thereabouts. So it was a huge drawdown.

claims.claim: The speaker states that from 2000 to 2012 or 2013, Microsoft would have been a very rough and bumpy ride, and he doesn't know anyone who would have held on.
claims.quote: And I don't know anyone who would have held on to their stock through that ride. And the NVIDIA situation today, so the history doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme.

claims.quote: It's now at a much higher valuation. So it's done really well. But I think from 2000 to 2012 or 2013, it would have been a very, very rough and bumpy ride.
